prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting in the theory of international trade, and showing how reallocation across firms shapes the gains from trade

statement.case_for: After reading the openings, I keep B001 first. Nine of eleven members rank it first and the other two rank it second, but I do not treat that as evidence of merit. The case rests on content. Melitz (2003) and Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) moved trade analysis from sectors to firms and produced sharp predictions that could be tested in firm-level data. Those predictions were tested repeatedly in administrative and customs microdata across many countries. This is the credibility-oriented pattern I value: a clear mechanism, testable implications, and a large body of evidence that confirmed the core selection and reallocation channel and refined it where it failed. More than twenty years of use in trade-liberalisation and productivity evaluation make the case mature. Attribution to Melitz and Helpman is cleaner than for any other broad candidate with similar reach, because the central model is Melitz's and the exporting-versus-FDI margin and the earlier monopolistic-competition foundations are Helpman's. The two-name configuration leaves no obvious gap among the credited names.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and identification. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made closely related contributions, and none of them is a credited name on this ballot entry. The committee would be crediting a theoretical framework while the empirical facts on exporter premia and the quantification of welfare gains came partly from others. The baseline Melitz model is also rejected in some details, for example in the Pareto-based welfare formulas and in the pattern of firm-level responses. The welfare conclusions therefore depend on auxiliary distributional assumptions. Trade was also recognised in 2008, and some members may weigh the field's recent representation against it. I judge these concerns real but not decisive. The citation should stay narrow, naming selection and reallocation as the discovery, rather than implying that the quantitative welfare magnitudes are settled.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B006 (BLP and dynamic industry models) first because the methods are mature, routine in antitrust and merger review, and influential well beyond industrial organisation, with a clean BLP core of Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes.
responses.response: I agree on maturity, reach and the cleanliness of the BLP core, which is why I ranked B006 second and keep it as an alternative. Two things keep me on B001. First, B006 is mainly a toolkit, and its credibility rests on functional-form and instrument assumptions. The credit boundary with Bresnahan, Reiss and the dynamic-games authors is also looser than the Melitz-Helpman boundary. Second, B001 delivered a conceptual change in what trade theory says about gains and winners, and it also generated tests that the data could confirm or reject. I would not discount B006 for being methodological, but I weigh substantive reorientation of a field somewhat more here.

responses.point: Krusell argues that two laureates give the cleanest attribution for B001, since Redding's quantitative and spatial work is a more derivative extension of the Melitz-Helpman core, and that the framework complements the earlier new-trade-theory prize without duplicating it.
responses.response: I largely agree and propose the same two names. I would qualify one point. Much of the evidence that makes the gains-from-trade claims usable comes from later quantitative work, and Redding is credited on the ballot. Leaving him out is defensible because the discovery is selection and reallocation, not quantification. But the citation should say so explicitly, so the committee does not appear to endorse the quantitative welfare estimates. I also take his point on the 2008 prize. The firm-heterogeneity step is distinct from the earlier scale-economies framework.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B001 first but flags that the committee might prefer a three-person split that adds Redding or the Bernard-Jensen empirical pioneers, who are not on the ballot.
responses.response: I take the attribution worry seriously, since the empirical exporter-premia facts that motivated the theory came from outside the credited set. But the committee can only credit names on this ballot entry. Bernard and Jensen are not credited here, so adding them is not an option I can propose. Adding Redding would blur the discovery rather than complete it. I would keep the pair, narrow the citation to the theoretical contribution, and treat the missing empirical pioneers as a recognised limitation, not a reason to widen the award.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B030 second and notes that a three-name limit forces a choice between the technology strand (Autor, Katz) and the trade-shock strand (Hanson, Dorn). He also notes that the persistence and interpretation of the trade-shock effects are still debated.
responses.response: This matches my own uncertainty about B030, which I ranked third. The China-shock design is the kind of quasi-experimental evidence I find most convincing about what is identified. But what it identifies is local labour-market adjustment to import exposure, which is narrower than the task-based claims about technology. Combining the two strands under one citation risks overstating how much one body of evidence supports the other. That is part of why B001 stays ahead of B030 for me, and why B030 is an alternative and not a co-recipient. If the committee prefers a labour-market prize, I would favour Autor, Hanson and Katz, with the caveat on Dorn versus Katz stated openly.

uncertainties: How much weight the committee gives to Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not credited on this ballot entry, when judging whether the Helpman-Melitz pair completes the attribution.
Whether the 2008 trade prize should reduce the field's claim to a second award this soon.
How much of the welfare-gain interpretation survives once the distributional assumptions of the baseline model are relaxed.
Whether Redding's quantitative contribution should be credited alongside or instead of Helpman. I currently think not, but the line is arguable.
I have not independently verified citation counts or priority records. My assessment rests on the openings and on general knowledge.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My co-authors and institutional ties (Uppsala, IFAU, Stockholm University) are in labour and education economics, and none of the credited names on B001 is among them. I overlapped with the IIES macro group at Stockholm University, but that was an institutional overlap and not a collaboration.
